Westphalia
west-FAY-lee-a
n. (the north-west German region of the Munster kingdom of 1534 and of the peace of 1648 that ended the wars of religion)
German Westfalen, the western Falen or plain-dwellers, as against the Ostfalen; Latin Westphalia.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Westphalia carries the Reformation's worst episode and its final settlement, both named after it. In 1534 and 1535 the city of Munster was seized by Melchiorite Anabaptists who proclaimed it the New Jerusalem, expelled all who would not be rebaptised, abolished private property, instituted polygamy, crowned the Dutch tailor Jan van Leiden as king, and held out through a siege that ended in starvation and the public torture of the leaders, whose bodies were hung in cages from the tower of St Lambert's church, where the cages remain. The episode was used for three centuries to discredit every form of believers' baptism, and it is the reason Menno Simons spent his life insisting on nonresistance. More than a century later, in the same region, the Peace of Westphalia was concluded at Munster and Osnabruck in 1648, ending the Thirty Years War, extending the Augsburg settlement to include the Reformed, and fixing the religious map of Germany. Westphalia also held real Reformed life: the academy at Steinfurt, and Philipp Nicolai, who wrote two of the greatest German hymns while burying a thousand of his people in a plague at Unna. The dictionary enters Westphalia because the same region holds the madness and the peace.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines a fanatic as one wild in religious opinions; polygamy as the having of more wives than one; a treaty as an agreement between nations; and a plague as a pestilence.

expand to see more

FANATIC, n. A person affected by excessive and unreasonable zeal, particularly in religious matters; an enthusiast.

POLYGAMY, n. A plurality of wives or husbands at the same time; the having of more than one wife at once.

TREATY, n. An agreement, league or contract between two or more nations or sovereigns, formally signed.

PLAGUE, n. A malignant contagious fever; a pestilence; any thing troublesome or vexatious.

CAGE, n. A box or enclosure made of boards or of wire, for confining birds or beasts.

Key Scripture

2Pe 2:1 — "But there were false prophets also among the people, even as there shall be false teachers among you, who privily shall bring in damnable heresies, even denying the Lord that bought them, and bring upon themselves swift destruction."

1Jo 4:1 — "Beloved, believe not every spirit, but try the spirits whether they are of God: because many false prophets are gone out into the world."

Mat 7:16 — "Ye shall know them by their fruits. Do men gather grapes of thorns, or figs of thistles?"

Jer 23:16 — "Thus saith the LORD of hosts, Hearken not unto the words of the prophets that prophesy unto you: they make you vain: they speak a vision of their own heart, and not out of the mouth of the LORD."

Modern Corruption

North-west German region where Anabaptist fanatics held Munster in 1534 and 1535, and where the Peace of 1648 ended the wars of religion.

expand to see more

The corruption to be named is the claim of fresh revelation, which produced at Munster every horror attributed to it. Jan Matthys and Jan van Leiden governed by dreams and prophecies, and from those prophecies came the expulsions, the common property, the polygamy and the crown. Scripture provides the test and the men of Munster failed it in public: “believe not every spirit, but try the spirits whether they are of God” (1Jo 4:1), and the prophet's word covers them exactly, that they “speak a vision of their own heart, and not out of the mouth of the LORD” (Jer 23:16).

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the testing of teachers by their doctrine and their lives, since “Ye shall know them by their fruits” (Mat 7:16), and the fruit at Munster was visible within a year. The dictionary also refuses the use Munster was put to: that false prophets arise within the church is foretold, for “there shall be false teachers among you” (2Pe 2:1), and their rising does not condemn the doctrine they corrupt. The peace signed in the same region in 1648 was not a triumph of truth but an exhaustion, and it gave the Reformed churches of the empire their legal standing.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek dokimazo (G1381), to test, to prove; Greek pseudodidaskalos (G5572), a false teacher; Hebrew chazon (H2377), a vision.

expand to see more

Greek dokimazo (G1381) — to test, to prove, to examine; “try the spirits whether they are of God”, 1 John 4:1.

Greek pseudodidaskalos (G5572) — a false teacher; “there shall be false teachers among you”, 2 Peter 2:1.

Greek karpos (G2590) — fruit, the produce of a tree or a life; “Ye shall know them by their fruits”, Matthew 7:16.

Hebrew chazon (H2377) — a vision, a revelation seen; “they speak a vision of their own heart”, Jeremiah 23:16.

Hebrew leb (H3820) — the heart, the inner man; “a vision of their own heart”, Jeremiah 23:16.

Usage

"“try the spirits whether they are of God” (1Jo 4:1) — Munster governed by dreams, 1534 and 1535."

"“they speak a vision of their own heart, and not out of the mouth of the LORD” (Jer 23:16) — a tailor crowned king of the New Jerusalem."

"“there shall be false teachers among you” (2Pe 2:1) — three centuries of using Munster against believers' baptism."
